theme: Cities of refuge; Levitical cities; the eastern tribes’ altar
readingInstruction: Read Joshua 20:1-22:34. Three episodes fill these chapters: the cities of refuge, the cities given to the Levites, and the near-disaster of the altar built by the eastern tribes. Read the cities of refuge with Hebrews 6:18 in mind, and read the altar story as a lesson in how God’s people handle misunderstanding.
settingTheScene: The land has been divided, and there are some important administrative matters left. God had commanded Moses to set up cities of refuge, places where someone who had killed another person accidentally could flee for protection from the avenger of blood. The Levites, who received no tribal territory, are given towns and pasturelands. And then the eastern tribes, Reuben, Gad, and half of Manasseh, who had helped the others conquer the land, are sent home. On the way, they build a large altar by the Jordan, and the rest of Israel prepares for civil war. The chapters show a nation learning to live in the land under God’s law, and the dangers of misunderstanding within the covenant family.
observation: God tells Joshua to “appoint the cities of refuge, of which I spoke to you through Moses” (20:2).
A person who killed “without intent” could flee to a city of refuge and stand before the elders at the gate (20:3-6).
The six cities are spread across the land, three on each side of the Jordan (20:7-9).
The man could stay there until the death of the high priest who was in office at the time (20:6).
Forty-eight cities with pasturelands are given to the Levites (21:1-42).
“Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed; all came to pass” (21:45).
The eastern tribes build “an altar of imposing size” by the Jordan, and the western tribes gather at Shiloh “to go up against them in war” (22:10-12).
Phinehas leads a delegation, and the eastern tribes explain that the altar is a witness, not a place for sacrifice (22:21-29, 34).
interpretation:
The cities of refuge are an expression of both justice and mercy. The law required that a murderer be put to death, but it also recognized that not every killing is murder. If someone killed another by accident, the avenger of blood could still pursue him, and the refuge was there to protect him. The elders of the city would hear his case, and he would be shielded until a proper trial. And the release came with the death of the high priest. This is one of the most interesting details in the whole system. The high priest’s death brings freedom for those who are confined. The author of Hebrews uses this kind of reasoning, because the death of our great high priest gives freedom to all who have fled to him for refuge. The six cities were also placed so that no one was too far from one. In Christ, the refuge is always near.

The Levite cities show God’s care for those who serve him. They do not hold a block of land, but they live among every tribe, as teachers and priests, so that the whole nation would be reached. The summary in 21:43-45 is among the most important statements in the book. “Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed; all came to pass.” The narrator pauses to record God’s faithfulness. It is a statement that is both historic and prophetic, since the story of Judges will immediately show the tragic ways Israel fails. But God does not fail.

Chapter 22 is a drama of near catastrophe. The eastern tribes erect an altar, and the western tribes assume it is rebellion. They are ready to go to war, and they cite Peor and Achan as precedents. But first they send a delegation, led by Phinehas, who is a priest and the zealous son of Eleazar. The meeting is a model of conflict resolution. The delegates come with questions and with a genuine concern for the covenant. The eastern tribes reply by explaining their motive. They had feared that future generations of western Israel would say, “You have no portion in the LORD.” The altar was built as a witness that they too belong to Israel. Phinehas and the leaders are satisfied, and the potential war is replaced by a blessing. The altar is named “Witness.”

The lesson is twofold. Zeal for God must be married to listening. And the unity of God’s people depends on honest communication. Division is often the result of assumptions. Many church conflicts could be avoided if believers followed the pattern of Phinehas, who went and asked before acting.
connection: The law of refuge appears in Numbers 35 and Deuteronomy 19. Hebrews 6:18 speaks of those who “have fled for refuge” to lay hold of the hope in Christ. The Levite cities fulfill Numbers 35:1-8. Joshua 21:45 is echoed in 23:14 and 1 Kings 8:56. The earlier eastern tribes’ agreement is in Numbers 32. The reference to Peor and Achan recalls Numbers 25 and Joshua 7. Matthew 18:15-20 gives a New Testament pattern for dealing with conflict.
application:
First, take refuge. If you feel guilt or fear, remember that Christ is a city of refuge for those who run to him. Take a specific burden to him today and rest there.

Second, consider whom you might be misjudging. Is there a person or a group you have assumed the worst about? Before acting, follow Phinehas: go and ask. Choose one relationship where a direct and gracious conversation could clear the air.

Third, receive the testimony of verse 45. Write it on a card: “Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made… had failed.” Read it when you are tempted to doubt.
prayerPrompts: Run to Christ with your guilt, and tell him what it is.
Ask him to make you quick to ask before you accuse.
Thank him for being your city of refuge.
